questions.q: On the loss landscape, what does the **global minimum** represent?
options: Any point where the surface looks flat
The lowest objective value anywhere on the landscape
The point where the weights are guaranteed to be unique and generalize best
The highest peak, where the model guesses most wildly
questions.explain: It is the lowest altitude on the whole map. Reaching it minimizes this objective, but the page stresses it does not necessarily give unique weights or guarantee the best generalization; flat points can also be saddles or local minima.

questions.q: You add a constant $5$ to every loss value of the landscape (shift it straight up). What happens to the location $(w_1, w_2)$ of the minimum?
options: It disappears because all values are now positive
questions.explain: The vertical offset is arbitrary: only differences in objective value shape the surface. Shifting everything up changes the altitude readout but not where the valleys and peaks are.

questions.q: A valley has very **steep walls**. What does that tell you?
options: The loss barely reacts to the weights there
The valley must be the global minimum
The optimizer will wander aimlessly there
Small changes in the weights cause large changes in the loss
questions.explain: Steepness = sensitivity: a tiny move in $w$ produces a big jump in loss. Flat regions are the opposite, where the optimizer may wander aimlessly because the slope gives little guidance.

questions.q: What does the gradient tell a model with billions of weights, whose landscape we cannot see?
options: The exact location of the global minimum
How many valleys the landscape has
The local direction of steepest increase, so we step the opposite way
Which weights can safely be deleted
questions.explain: Like a hiker in fog feeling the slope underfoot, the gradient only provides local information. Gradient descent steps opposite to it, with no guarantee of finding the global minimum.
